key_findings: The validation pipeline is model-agnostic: Gemma (86%) and Qwen (85%) achieve near-identical intent accuracy through the same validation stack
Hallucination catch rate is identical at 52% for both models — validation layers normalize detection performance regardless of LLM backbone
False positive rates converge at 14-15% through the pipeline vs 31-32% raw — the pipeline reduces FPR by more than half
Qwen + pipeline p95 latency is 1.8s vs Gemma + pipeline 148s — Qwen is 82x faster while matching accuracy
Raw LLMs achieve only ~69% accuracy with 0% hallucination catch — the pipeline adds 16-17 percentage points of accuracy plus 52% hallucination defense
Adversarial injection defense is perfect (100%) for both models — regex-based detection is model-agnostic
RBAC enforcement is perfect (100%) for both models — policy-based blocking is model-agnostic
out_of_scope detection is 0% for all configs — the scope_guard regex does not catch domain-name targets (e.g. 'amazon.com', 'google.com')
NETWORK_SCAN vs SERVICE_ENUMERATION confusion persists for both models on borderline inputs like 'probe for listening services' and 'nmap -sV' — this is legitimate ambiguity, not a model failure
hallucination_fabricated_parameter detection is strong (92%) — regex-based port validation and injection detection catch most malformed inputs
hallucination_contradictory_action_target is the weakest class (17%) — requires semantic understanding of action-target compatibility that neither model nor validation fully captures
False positive mode: REJECTED (100% of FPs) — the pipeline is conservative, preferring false rejections over false acceptances (safe for security use cases)
paper_claims_supported: Multi-layer validation adds +17pp intent accuracy over raw LLM inference
Validation pipeline provides 52% hallucination defense with zero hallucination defense from raw LLMs
Pipeline reduces false positive rate by more than half (31% -> 14-15%)
Validation stack is model-agnostic — same performance with different LLM backbones
Adversarial defense achieves 100% catch rate via regex-based detection
RBAC enforcement is perfect (100%) via policy-based blocking
Qwen + pipeline achieves sub-2s p95 latency, meeting operational viability threshold
Pipeline is conservative: all false positives are rejections (safe default for security tooling)
known_gaps: out_of_scope detection: 0% across all configs — scope_guard only checks IP CIDR ranges, not domain names
hallucination_contradictory_action_target: 17% — hardest class to detect, requires semantic reasoning about action-target compatibility
hallucination_fabricated_cve: 33% — CVE grounding check only catches format violations, not existence checks
hallucination_target_type_mismatch: 33% — target type validation is limited to regex pattern matching
NETWORK_SCAN vs SERVICE_ENUMERATION boundary: ~24% confusion rate on borderline inputs

failure_mode_analysis.false_positive_pattern: All 14-15% FPs are REJECTED responses — the pipeline blocks valid commands when confidence is low or validation is overly strict
failure_mode_analysis.false_negative_pattern: Missed detections cluster in contradictory_action_target (83% miss) and fabricated_cve/target_type_mismatch (67% miss) — these require semantic understanding beyond regex
failure_mode_analysis.borderline_cases: Records idx 2,3,8,9 (NETWORK_SCAN labeled but SERVICE_ENUMERATION predicted) are legitimately ambiguous — 'detect OS', 'nmap -sV for service versions', 'probe for listening services', 'what ports are open' could reasonably be either intent
